name: Picurís
confidence_why: Zaharlick 1977, restating the only first-hand phonology of Picurís (F. H. Trager 1968, 1971), treats word stress as a morphemic stress pattern with no positional rule (/píwene/ 'rabbit' against /pìwénę̀/ 'rabbits'), but Sutton 2014 calls that three-stress, three-tone framework "highly suspect", suggests that some of what is marked as stress is really tone, and offers no alternative placement while labelling his own reanalysis speculative.

catalog_quote: 2.5. Besides the vowel and consonant phonemes, the Picurls language has three phonemes of stress: primary / ' /, secondary /"/, and weak / w/, which will generally be left unmarked. Stress refers to the prominence of a syllable. In Picurls, stress refers to the loudness and length of the vowel nucleus, or, in some cases where the stressed syllable ends in /I m n/, the final consonant, rather than the vowel nucleus, evidences lengthening. ... Important to the structure of this language are the numerous stress sequences. Thus, /plwene/ 'rabbit' contrasts in pattern with /piwSn^/ 'rabbits'. In this example and many like it, it is the stress patterns ... that are the important marks of contrast. tone_statements.citation: Zaharlick, Amy. 1982. Tanoan Studies: Passive Sentences in Picuris. Ohio State University Working Papers in Linguistics 26: 34-48. hdl:1811/81458
tone_statements.quote: There are three tones in Picuris: low, middle, and high. In terms of occurrence, middle tone is the most frequent and high tone is the least frequent. High and low tones occur primarily on base morphemes. A few suffixes, however, have high tone, but prefixes and suffixes are mostly tone neutral structurally. Although most prefixes and suffixes have middle tone phonemically, a slight rise or decline in pitch phonetically is anticipatory for prefixes with following base tone and residual for suffixes with preceding base tone.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (low, middle, high) alongside three contrastive stress phonemes; high and low mainly on base morphemes, affixes mostly middle; primary stress raises tone pitch. Texts unmarked.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so no direct conflict with it can be stated. Among the witnesses already held by the project there is a real disagreement in type: Zaharlick 1977 (following F. H. Trager 1968/1971) §2.5, p.31-32, gives Picurís 'three phonemes of stress: primary, secondary [medial], and weak' alongside three tones, states that '/píwene/ "rabbit" contrasts in pattern with /pìwénę̀/ "rabbits"' and that 'the stress system, therefore, is one of contrasting word superfixes, with the three levels of stress occurring in different sequences', and on p.48 concludes that stress placement is 'morphemic rather than phonological' (i.e. lexical, no positional rule). Sutton 2014 §6.5.1.3, p.420, says 'the status and details of tone in Picuris Tiwa are uncertain. The only available published analysis is formulated under the same rubric as George Trager's description of Taos Tiwa, a system I find highly suspect', expects instead a three-tone system like Taos (Hull 1973), and on p.421 says Nichols 1994's stress-based account of noun-suffix allomorphy is 'more likely.. based on tone'. So the Trager/Zaharlick tradition treats Picurís as having contrastive lexical stress plus tone, while Sutton treats the prominence contrasts as tone and doubts that stress is a separate contrastive category.

sources.citation: Sutton, Logan. 2014. Kiowa-Tanoan: A Synchronic and Diachronic Study. Ph.D. dissertation, University of New Mexico.https://digitalrepository.unm.edu/ling_etds/34
sources.quote: No independent Picuris stress analysis; treats the Trager/Zaharlick three-stress-three-tone system as suspect, suggests a Hull-type three-tone (high/low/falling) system with stress independent, reinterprets some 'medial stress' markings on noun suffixes as high tone, and generalises that KT lexical stress tends to be stem-initial; explicitly calls all of this speculative pending work with recordings/speakers.
